explanations.answer: The men of Hezekiah king of Judah
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says these are additional proverbs of Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), and that they were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). Somebody had to sit down and copy them all out. I think that took real patience, and I get nervous just carrying a full tray across the kitchen.

explanations.answer: The men of Josiah king of Judah
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not the name in the verse. Proverbs 25:1 says the men of Hezekiah king of Judah did the copying. These are additional proverbs of Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), and Hezekiah's men copied them. Royal names run together fast, and I once grabbed the wrong cookie sheet just like that.

explanations.answer: The men of Jehoshaphat king of Judah
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Proverbs 25:1 names the men of Hezekiah king of Judah as the ones who copied these proverbs of Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1). It's a long name, so I get why it sticks in the head. Hezekiah is the name to hold onto here.

That's it, friend. "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out." (Proverbs 25:2) God conceals a matter, and kings get glory from searching it out. Searching takes effort. I think a little digging is just fine.

Good guess, friend, but the verse gives kings a different job. The glory of God is to conceal a matter, and the glory of kings is "…to search it out." (Proverbs 25:2) Kings are the searchers, not the sealers.

A loud announcement sounds very kingly, I'll give you that. But Solomon says something else: the glory of God is to conceal a matter, and the glory of kings is "…to search it out." (Proverbs 25:2) Kings go looking. They don't just shout.

Yes, their hearts. "As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched." (Proverbs 25:3) That's about as far as you can go in both directions. Nobody gets to the bottom of it.

Treasures are a good guess, friend, since kings are known for those. But the verse says the hearts of kings cannot be searched (Proverbs 25:3). Solomon puts it next to the high heavens and the deep earth. That's a lot of distance.

Borders sound like something a king could be asked about, and I get why you picked it. But Proverbs 25:3 says it's the hearts of kings that cannot be searched. The comparison is the high heavens and the deep earth, which is a long way up and a long way down.

That's the word. "Remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness." (Proverbs 25:5) Same as the silver, where you take out the dross first. Clear the wicked out and the throne stands on solid ground.

No, friend, the verse doesn't send the poor away. Solomon says to remove the wicked from the king's presence (Proverbs 25:5). The line sits right after the silver and its dross, so the picture is about taking out what spoils the metal. The wicked are what gets taken out.

Strangers get a warm welcome in my bakery, so I'm glad that's not what the verse says. Solomon says to remove the wicked from the king's presence (Proverbs 25:5). The line is about removing the wicked, not about who is new.

Right on. With the wicked removed from his presence, the king's throne "…will be established in righteousness." (Proverbs 25:5) A throne set on that holds firm. I wish my wobbly baking table could say the same.

Wealth is a good guess, friend, but it's not in the verse. Once the wicked are removed from the king's presence, his throne "…will be established in righteousness." (Proverbs 25:5) The foundation is righteousness. Gold doesn't come up.

Fear does hold up a lot of thrones in the world, I'll give you that. But this verse says the throne will be established in righteousness after the wicked are removed from the king's presence (Proverbs 25:5). That's the foundation Solomon names.

explanations.answer: Demoted in front of the prince
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "…it is better to be told, “Come up here!” than to be demoted in the presence of the prince." (Proverbs 25:7) Getting invited up beats getting sent down. Solomon would rather you wait for the invitation than grab the seat yourself. I think walking back down from the big seat has to be the longest walk there is.

explanations.answer: Ignored in front of the crowd
explanations.explanation: Ignored would sting, no doubt. But the verse says it's better to be told "Come up here!" than to be "…demoted in the presence of the prince." (Proverbs 25:7) The problem Solomon names is being demoted, right in front of the prince.

explanations.answer: Questioned in front of the judges
explanations.explanation: Court comes up in the very next verse, friend, but this verse doesn't mention judges. Solomon says it's better to be told "Come up here!" than to be "…demoted in the presence of the prince." (Proverbs 25:7) Demoted in front of the prince is the line.

True. Solomon asks what you'll do in the end "…when your neighbor puts you to shame?" (Proverbs 25:8) That's the risk of bringing something hastily to court, even something you saw with your own eyes. Slow down before you take it that far.

It's true, friend. The text warns not to bring something hastily to court, and then asks, "Otherwise, what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame?" (Proverbs 25:8) Even what you've seen with your own eyes isn't a reason to rush. Hurrying is where the shame comes in.

Not this time, friend. Solomon says to argue your case with your neighbor "…without betraying another’s confidence…" (Proverbs 25:9) So spilling someone else's secret is off the table, even when it would help you win. The text puts a limit on how you argue.

False is right. The verse says to argue your case with your neighbor "…without betraying another’s confidence…" (Proverbs 25:9) You can make your argument, but another person's secret isn't yours to spend. Win or lose, that door stays closed.

Yes, friend. "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver." (Proverbs 25:11) The right word at the right time is a treasure, like gold set in silver. Solomon is talking about what we say, not what we own. I think that's rarer than a perfectly even batch, and I work hard on those.

A secret gift sounds lovely, but the verse is about something else. Proverbs 25:11 says "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver." The gold and silver picture belongs to a well-spoken word. It's a gift made of words.

A house on rock is a strong picture, friend, but it's not this one. Solomon says "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver." (Proverbs 25:11) Here the treasure is a word spoken well. You don't need any bricks for it.

That's the one. "Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man’s rebuke to a listening ear." (Proverbs 25:12) A listening ear is what makes the rebuke worth wearing. I think a stubborn ear would just leave the jewelry in the box.

Royal sounds fancy enough for gold, and I understand the pick. But the verse says a wise man's rebuke is like gold jewelry "…to a listening ear." (Proverbs 25:12) The ear Solomon names is a listening one, not a royal one.
Foreign ears show up in a lot of places, but not here. Proverbs 25:12 says a wise man's rebuke is like gold jewelry "…to a listening ear." The ear that makes the difference is the one that listens.

True, friend. You read that one right. "Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters." (Proverbs 25:13) That's the picture Solomon chooses for a trustworthy messenger. The ones who send him are the ones who get refreshed.

It's true, friend. Proverbs 25:13 says a trustworthy messenger is like "…the cold of snow in the time of harvest…" to those who send him. He "…refreshes the soul of his masters." Snow in harvest is the picture Solomon chose for how refreshing that messenger is.

explanations.answer: The man who boasts of gifts never given
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given." (Proverbs 25:14) Big talk, lots of promise, and then nothing falls. Clouds without rain are all show. Solomon's point is that a boast means little without a gift behind it.

explanations.answer: The man who hides his silver in the ground
explanations.explanation: Hiding silver is a different story, friend. Proverbs 25:14 says the man like clouds and wind without rain is "…the man who boasts of gifts never given." Clouds and wind promise rain and then deliver none. That's the picture of a boast with no gift behind it.

explanations.answer: The man who sleeps through the harvest
explanations.explanation: Sleeping through harvest is a rough day at work, but it's not in this verse. Proverbs 25:14 says it's "…the man who boasts of gifts never given." who is like clouds and wind without rain. The empty sky matches the empty promise.

Not true, friend. Solomon says "Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone." (Proverbs 25:15) So a gentle tongue is no weakling. It's strong enough to break a bone.

False, and the verse says it plainly. "Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone." (Proverbs 25:15) A gentle tongue has real power. Soft words can do more than you'd think.
Yes, that's what the verse says. "If you find honey, eat just what you need, lest you have too much and vomit it up." (Proverbs 25:16) Not pretty, but honest. Take what you need and leave the rest.
A nap is a gentler ending, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. Proverbs 25:16 says "…lest you have too much and vomit it up." Solomon doesn't soften it. Eat just what you need.

Losing strength is a fair guess for a sugar crash, but the text says something else. Proverbs 25:16 says eat just what you need, "…lest you have too much and vomit it up." That's the consequence Solomon gives.

Not quite, friend. Solomon says "Seldom set foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he grow weary and hate you." (Proverbs 25:17) More visits can wear a neighbor out, and love isn't the result. A little space goes a long way.
False is right. The verse says "Seldom set foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he grow weary and hate you." (Proverbs 25:17) Too many visits can leave a neighbor tired of you. Keep it seldom.

explanations.answer: A man who bears false witness against his neighbor
explanations.explanation: That's the one. "Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor." (Proverbs 25:18) Three weapons, all for a lie told about a neighbor. Words can hurt like they have an edge.

explanations.answer: A man who moves his neighbor's boundary stone
explanations.explanation: Moving a boundary stone is a different kind of wrongdoing, friend, and it's not in this verse. Proverbs 25:18 says the club, the sword and the sharp arrow match "…a man who bears false witness against his neighbor." The weapons go with the false witness.

explanations.answer: A man who borrows and never pays it back
explanations.explanation: A borrower who never pays back is frustrating, I'll admit. But Proverbs 25:18 puts the club, the sword and the sharp arrow with "…a man who bears false witness against his neighbor." The weapon picture is about harmful words.

Yes, friend. "Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble." (Proverbs 25:19) You lean on him when you need him most, and he gives out. That's the pain Solomon is describing. Faithless is the word that fills the blank.

Wealth doesn't make it into this verse, friend. Proverbs 25:19 says the broken tooth and the foot out of joint match "…confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble." It's faithlessness that lets you down, not money.
A quiet man gets a pass here. Proverbs 25:19 says confidence in "…a faithless man in time of trouble." is like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint. The problem Solomon names is the faithless one.

Yes, friend. "Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart." (Proverbs 25:20) Solomon pictures a cold day with the garment gone, and a wound with vinegar poured in. Songs aimed at someone who is hurting just add to the sting. I think sometimes the kind thing is to say less.

Sitting quietly isn't what the verse warns against, friend. Proverbs 25:20 says the cold-day garment and the vinegar on a wound match "…one who sings songs to a heavy heart." The song is the problem here.

Weeping with someone isn't the one Solomon names, friend. Proverbs 25:20 says it's "…one who sings songs to a heavy heart." who is like a garment removed on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound. So the verse points at the singing.

That's it, friend. "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat…" (Proverbs 25:21) Solomon says it plainly, with no list of conditions. A hungry enemy is still hungry. Giving the food is the instruction.
No waiting period in this verse, friend. Proverbs 25:21 says "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat…" Solomon doesn't mention asking even once, let alone twice.
Passing the job along would be easier, I know. But Proverbs 25:21 says "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat…" The instruction is to give it yourself.
Yes. The verse says "…and the LORD will reward you." (Proverbs 25:22) That's the line right after the burning coals. Caring for an enemy is something the LORD rewards.

A king would be a fine one to hear from, friend, but the verse names someone else. Proverbs 25:22 says "…and the LORD will reward you." Feeding an enemy isn't easy, I think, so it matters who Solomon says does the rewarding. The reward comes from the LORD, not from a throne.

Neighbors came up earlier in the chapter, friend, but not here. Proverbs 25:22 says "…and the LORD will reward you." Verse 21 has you giving food and water to an enemy, and this verse says who does the rewarding. I think that's good news, because you don't have to wait around for anybody's thank-you.

That's right, friend. "As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks." (Proverbs 25:23) A backbiting tongue brings angry looks, the way the north wind brings rain. Talk behind someone's back, and the faces change. Just like the weather, you can see it coming.

Pride does cause its share of trouble, friend, but it's not in this verse. Proverbs 25:23 says "As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks." The tongue is what Solomon names.
An empty purse can put anyone in a mood, I'll grant you. But Proverbs 25:23 says "…so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks." The tongue that bites behind someone's back is the cause here.

explanations.answer: Sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife." (Proverbs 25:24) A corner of the roof sounds cramped, but Solomon says it's better. He's saying a quarrelsome home is hard to live in. I think constant arguing wears everyone down.

A prison cell is a rough comparison, but it's not what the verse says. Proverbs 25:24 says it's better to live on a corner of the roof "…than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife." The comparison is a quarrelsome house.

explanations.answer: Living in a tent in the desert
explanations.explanation: A desert tent doesn't appear here, friend. Proverbs 25:24 says living on a corner of the roof is better "…than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife." That's the one Solomon compares it to.

True, friend. "Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land." (Proverbs 25:25) Good news from far away refreshes a weary soul the way cold water does. Solomon's picture is a cool drink for someone worn out. I think a cold drink does the same for a tired body.
It's true, friend. Proverbs 25:25 says "Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land." Good news from far away can lift a weary soul the way cold water does.

Not this time. Solomon says "Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way to the wicked." (Proverbs 25:26) The picture is a righteous man giving way, not standing up. A spring should run clean.

False is right. The verse says the muddied spring or polluted well is "…a righteous man who gives way to the wicked." (Proverbs 25:26) It's the giving way that spoils the water. Standing firm is the opposite picture.

Yes, friend. "It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory." (Proverbs 25:27) Solomon puts the two side by side. He says it's not good to eat too much honey. In the same breath, he says it's not good to search out your own glory.

Asking for advice is a good move, friend, so it's not what this verse warns about. Proverbs 25:27 says "It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory." The warning is about searching out your own glory.

Rest after hard work isn't the target here, I'm glad to say. Proverbs 25:27 says "It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory." The second thing named is searching out your own glory.

That's the word. "Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper." (Proverbs 25:28) Walls keep a city safe, and a man without control of his temper has nothing to hold things back. I've had my own hot moments over burnt batches.

Money can get out of control for plenty of people, but it's not the word here. Proverbs 25:28 says "Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper." The walls are about the temper.
Servants aren't mentioned in this verse, friend. Proverbs 25:28 says the city with broken walls is like "…a man who does not control his temper." The thing he can't control is his own temper.
